h1: Reading a beer specification sheet when you are not a brewer
title: Reading a Beer Specification Sheet | Craft Beer School
desc: A plain guide to a beer specification sheet: ABV, gravity, colour, bitterness, CO2, oxygen, pH and haze, with what each number means for the drinker.
teaser: ABV, °P, EBC, IBU, ppb. The spec sheet looks like a lab report. Each line is really a promise to the drinker.
standfirst: Every beer a brewery sells has a specification: a list of measured values with targets and limits. If you work in quality data, planning, marketing or supply without a brewing background, this guide will help you read one and know which numbers matter most.
sections:
A beer specification sheet defines what a brand should be when it leaves the brewery. Each parameter has a target and a tolerance, usually a minimum and maximum. A batch inside every limit can be released. A batch outside a limit is held, blended, reworked or rejected. Our guide to how a beer batch is released covers that decision.

The point of the sheet is consistency. Drinkers expect the same beer every time. The spec turns that expectation into numbers a lab can measure.

• Alcohol (ABV). Percentage alcohol by volume. It must match what the label declares within the tolerance the rules allow, so this is a legal number as well as a quality one.
  • Original gravity (OG), often in degrees Plato (°P). How much sugar and other dissolved material the wort held before fermentation. Roughly, 1 °P is about 1% dissolved extract by weight. More extract means more potential alcohol and body.
  • Apparent and real extract. What is left after fermentation. Higher residual extract usually means a fuller, sweeter beer. The difference between original and final extract tells you how far the yeast fermented.

Large breweries often brew at high gravity and dilute to final strength. That is why OG on a spec sheet can refer to the beer as sold rather than the wort in the kettle.

• Colour, in EBC units. A pale lager sits in single figures. Amber beers run into the twenties and thirties. Stouts go well past 100.
  • Bitterness, in IBU or EBU. Roughly the concentration of bitter hop compounds in milligrams per litre. A mainstream Indian lager is low, often in the teens. An IPA can be 40 to 70 or more.
  • Haze, in EBC haze units. How clear the beer is. A filtered lager will have a tight upper limit. A wheat beer or hazy IPA is meant to be cloudy and may have no haze limit at all.
  • pH. Finished beer is acidic, typically about 4.0 to 4.6. A drift outside the brand's normal band can point to a fermentation or infection problem.

Two lines protect the beer after it leaves the brewery.

  • Carbon dioxide (CO2), in grams per litre or volumes. Most lagers are around 5 g/L, roughly 2.5 volumes. Too low and the beer tastes flat. Too high and it gushes or tastes sharp.
  • Dissolved oxygen in the package, in parts per billion (ppb). Oxygen is the enemy of shelf life. Good packaging lines aim for very low figures, often below 100 ppb in the finished pack. A creeping oxygen number usually shows up as stale beer months later.

Some sheets add foam stability (often a timed test in seconds), diacetyl (a buttery fermentation by-product with a limit in fractions of a milligram per litre) and microbiology results. Each one exists because it has caused real complaints somewhere.
How to read it like a brewer

Brewers do not read a spec sheet line by line. They read it for patterns.

  • One value just inside its limit is normal variation. Several values drifting in the same direction over weeks is a process change worth chasing.
  • Strength, extract and CO2 tend to move with each other because they come from the same fermentation and packaging steps.
  • A pass on every line does not guarantee a good beer. Taste panels catch faults instruments miss, which is why most breweries pair the spec with a sensory check.

If you work with these numbers in dashboards, our guide to beer quality data for data teams goes further into trends and control charts.
Where the brewhouse floor shows up

Every line on the sheet maps to a step you could walk to. Bitterness depends on hop additions in the kettle. CO2 is set in the bright beer tank before packaging. Oxygen pick-up happens at the filler, where a poorly adjusted fill height or a worn seal can quietly push numbers up for a whole shift.

Learning that map is what turns a table of numbers into something a planner or analyst can act on. It is also the part a slide deck cannot teach: you understand oxygen when you have smelt a stale bottle next to a fresh one.
faqs: What is the most important number on a beer spec sheet?
Alcohol, because it is a legal declaration as well as a quality value. For shelf life, dissolved oxygen in the package matters most.
Why do some beers have no haze limit?
Styles such as wheat beer and hazy IPA are meant to be cloudy. Their spec may control haze stability or appearance by panel instead of setting a maximum.
Degrees Plato, a measure of dissolved extract in wort or beer. One degree is roughly one percent extract by weight.
